newsitem.title: GERMANY: Greenpeace sees risks in EU-approved gene maize.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace sees risks in EU-approved gene maize.

text.p: Environmental group Greenpeace said gene-modified maize approved on Wednesday for sale in the European Union would increase human and animal resistance to the healing effects of antibiotics.
"Antibiotic resistance, which can be spread by this maize, may threaten the health of humans and animals," maize campaign co-ordinator Benny Haerlin of Greenpeace's Germany office told Reuters.
"We are outraged that Ciba Geigy AG will be allowed to render ineffective the value of a herbicide, which is currently environmentally neutral, over the next few years."
Approval of the grain by the EU Commission, with as yet unspecified labelling conditions, followed advice from three sets of EU scientists who said there were no reasons to ban the maize.

The gene-modified maize (corn) will be imported from the United States where farmers have planted the Ciba-developed variety, which is resistant to the herbicide glufosinate and the corn-borer pest and carries an antibiotic "marker gene."
Haerlin said the Commission had bowed to pressure from the biotechnology industry and the United States and legalised illegally imported maize which had already entered the EU.
"The decision was made although national authorities and scientists expressed grave concerns about health and environmental risks," he said.
"We will try to put pressure on national authorities to reverse the decision or at least not to implement it in their countries."
"We will also ask the feeds and food industries not to use genetically modified maize and its products."

Greenpeace would also keep a watchful eye on the implementation of the so-called novel food legislation in which Brussels laid down labelling rules for foods containing genetically modified organisms (GMOs).
Greenpeace says the law has too many loopholes and has vowed to keep up a fight against gene-altered United States soybeans, where it sees unknown health risks.
